title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Fireside chat with Ben Graham Centre on October 14, 2025
summary: A fireside chat on cloning as a life philosophy: Pabrai explains why humans refuse to clone, how he cloned Buffett's 0-6-25 partnership fee structure in 1999, and his late realization that a properly run portfolio ends up ~95% in one great business. He also covers asymmetric small bets, radical truthfulness from David Hawkins' Power vs. Force, the cloned Dakshana model and its latest IIT/AIIMS results, and the discipline of sitting quietly and doing nothing.

ideas.idea: Cloning is one of the most powerful mental models precisely because most humans have an evolutionary aversion to it and think it is beneath them.
ideas.detail: Herd-following aided survival in hunter-gatherer times, but people still resist copying proven ideas even when told to, so the edge endures. 'The world can accommodate three of the same thing'; almost everything that worked in his life was cloned.

ideas.idea: If you cannot explain an investment thesis in three sentences to a 10-year-old, something is wrong with the investment.
ideas.detail: He cites Einstein's four levels of intellect (smart, intelligent, genius, simple) with simplicity as the highest; boiling a cloned idea to its essence makes execution easy.

ideas.idea: He built Pabrai Funds in 1999 by cloning Buffett's 0-6-25 partnership fee structure, which nobody had copied in the 30 years since the partnership ended in 1969.
ideas.detail: 0% management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% of the upside is a win-win; he told early investors to put all family money only with zero-fee managers, making him a monopoly. Munger later said a few obscure people had cloned it. In 2025, 56 years on, he is still waiting for the cloners.

ideas.idea: 'Value investing' is a redundant term; all intelligent investing is value investing.
ideas.detail: There is no such thing as anything else, so it should just be called investing.

ideas.idea: He cloned Buffett badly for two decades by overdosing on Ben Graham and underdosing on Charlie Munger, yet even suboptimal cloning lands you in paradise.
ideas.detail: After 31 years following Buffett, he says the first 20 were 'in the wilderness' despite being friends with Warren and Charlie; he figured it out only seven or eight years ago.

ideas.idea: If the job is done right, your portfolio will end up 95% in one stock; a manager whose portfolio is not is not optimizing.
ideas.detail: Truly great businesses run by great managers are rare but will find their way into most portfolios; the key is to shut off the brain, ignore intrinsic-value calculations, and let a 2-10% position grow to 90% as long as business and manager stay good. His problem was being 'too much of an idiot to keep them'.

ideas.idea: Two businesses now make up close to 70% of one of his funds and he told investors he will not diversify or sell; those uncomfortable can redeem.
ideas.detail: He advised anyone with under 20% of net worth in the fund to leave it alone; nobody called or redeemed, and he expects the same at 90%.

ideas.idea: Most things he has tried, cloned or not, failed, but life's asymmetry means a few big winners pay for 50 failed side bets.
ideas.detail: Bezos understands asymmetry best: Amazon keeps making small bets, loses $50-200 million on most and moves on, but AWS was one of those throws against the wall. Try many things where the downside of failure is not meaningful.

ideas.idea: Eliminating white lies and preferring truth over diplomacy builds trust, which is a real edge in life, per David Hawkins' Power vs. Force.
ideas.detail: Hawkins argues the subconscious detects lies even when the conscious mind does not. Post-Hawkins he tells his wife when a dress doesn't work, taking short-term pain for a stronger relationship. Truth is on a log curve: Jesus, Buddha and Gandhi at the extreme, Buffett and Munger a bit below; Munger says the world runs on trust, not contracts.

ideas.idea: Dakshana is a cloned model, scaled from a Bihar math teacher's 30 students a year to 1,000, spending about $3,000 per student to get poor kids into IIT.
ideas.detail: He read about the teacher in BusinessWeek in 2006; the teacher got 90%+ of very poor students into IIT versus a sub-1% national admit rate (2 million test-takers for ~16,000 seats) but had no interest in scaling, so Pabrai asked to clone it. $3,000 moves a family from $1,000-2,000 a year to $100,000-200,000 via jobs at Google or Microsoft.

ideas.idea: Dakshana works because it leverages two free government systems, the IITs and the JNV magnet schools, giving a 60-to-1 or 70-to-1 subsidy on its spending.
ideas.detail: The IITs spend $50-60,000 a year per student and JNVs another $15-20,000, close to $250,000 per child in total, against Dakshana's $3,000. IIT Bombay Computer Science, which closes by rank 80, has more brainpower than any classroom at MIT or Stanford; Bill Gates said he would recruit only from IITs if limited to one school.

ideas.idea: Dakshana's medical track now places 25% of its students into AIIMS, which has a 0.1% admit rate, a 250x higher hit rate than the general population.
ideas.detail: Those who miss AIIMS get into other government medical colleges; AIIMS alumni like Deepak Chopra are among the best doctors in the world.

ideas.idea: His goal since 2006-07 is to be remembered for Dakshana rather than as an investor, and his daughter's Dakshana tattoo is his highest accomplishment as a dad.
ideas.detail: He says the goal is already largely met with about 30 years still to go.

ideas.idea: All investment manager misery stems from the inability to sit quietly in a room alone and do nothing; activity is the single biggest issue.
ideas.detail: He adapted Pascal's quote and says learning to enjoy watching paint dry took him a very long time and he is still trying to get better at it.

ideas.idea: There is no master plan; put one foot in front of the other and aspire to be a better investor, better at giving money away, and a good person for society.
ideas.detail: He describes the aim simply as leaving the planet a better place than he found it.
